Restraint of Sin
ri-STRAYNT uhv sin
doctrinal phrase
From restraint (a holding back, a check) and sin; the work of God’s common grace in curbing the outworking of human depravity.

📖 Biblical Definition

The restraint of sin is the work of God’s common grace by which He curbs and bridles the outworking of human depravity in the world, holding back fallen men from being as wicked as their corrupt nature would otherwise make them. Though all men are by nature totally depraved—corrupted in every part, dead in sin, and incapable of any saving good—they are not in this life as bad as they could be, because God restrains the full expression of their sin. He does this by many means: through the conscience, which accuses and excuses; through the natural affections of family and neighbor; through the fear of shame and punishment; through civil government, which He ordained to bear the sword against evildoers; and by the direct, secret operation of His Spirit upon the hearts of men, as He restrained Abimelech from touching Sarah and turned the counsel of the wicked. This restraint is not regeneration and works no saving change; it leaves the heart unrenewed and the man still under wrath. But it preserves order in society, makes human life possible, and serves God’s purposes of providence and the gathering of His church. The dictionary holds the restraint of sin as an important part of the doctrine of common grace, guarding two truths at once. It upholds total depravity, for the relative civic goodness of unbelievers is owing not to any soundness in their nature but to God’s restraining hand; and it accounts for the order and good found in a fallen world, which would otherwise be a hell of unchecked wickedness. When God lifts the restraint, as He sometimes does in judgment, giving men over to their sin, the depths of human corruption are laid bare.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

God’s common-grace work of curbing human depravity—through conscience, family, government, and His Spirit—so that fallen men are not as wicked as their nature would make them; it upholds total depravity while preserving order.

RESTRAINT OF SIN, God’s common-grace curbing of human depravity.

Holds back fallen men from being as wicked as their nature would make them.

Worked through conscience, family, fear, civil government, and the Spirit.

Not regeneration; it works no saving change but preserves order.

When God lifts it in judgment, the depths of human corruption appear.

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 20:6 — "And God said unto him in a dream, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her."

Psa 76:10 — "Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain."

Rom 13:4 — "For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Rom 1:24 — "Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The civic goodness of the unregenerate is mistaken for natural soundness, denying total depravity; or God’s restraining hand in society is forgotten.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the relative goodness found among unbelievers is owing not to any soundness in fallen human nature but to God’s restraining grace. The doctrine guards total depravity against the objection that unregenerate men often live decently and do civic good: they do so because God curbs the full expression of their corruption through conscience, affection, fear, and the sword of the magistrate, not because their nature is partly sound. Lift the restraint, and the same men are capable of every evil.

The opposite forgetfulness ignores God’s restraining hand in society altogether, taking the order and good of a fallen world for granted as if it were the natural state of man, rather than a mercy of common grace. The dictionary holds both truths: man is totally depraved, yet God in mercy restrains sin so that human life and society are possible and His church may be gathered. And it holds the solemn corollary: when God in judgment lifts the restraint and gives men over to their own hearts’ lusts, as Romans 1 describes, the true depths of human corruption are laid bare, and a society once orderly may descend swiftly into open wickedness.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase names God’s common-grace bridling of depravity, which upholds total depravity while preserving the order of a fallen world.

expand to see more

“Restraint” — a holding back, a check upon the outworking of sin.

A work of common grace, not of saving, regenerating grace.

Worked through conscience, natural affection, fear, and civil government.

Also by the Spirit’s direct operation, as He withheld Abimelech.

When lifted in judgment, God “gives men up” to their sin (Romans 1).

Usage

"The restraint of sin explains the civic good of the unregenerate without denying total depravity."

"It is part of the doctrine of common grace."

"God’s lifting of restraint in judgment is seen in Romans 1’s “gave them up.”"
